At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write the single sharpest follow-up question a teacher would ask next. Do not mention or quote the trace token. (trace-2317)
response:
When a tokenizer is trained on a corpus that mixes source code and natural language, the subword vocabulary it learns reflects statistical regularities from both domains simultaneously — but these domains have radically different character-level distributions, whitespace semantics, and repetition patterns. The central question is: how do the boundaries between subword tokens shift in ways that are systematic but non-obvious, and how do those shifts propagate into downstream model behavior? Key concepts include the BPE or Unigram merge priority ordering, vocabulary fertility (tokens-per-word ratio across domains), and boundary misalignment — where a token learned primarily from code context gets applied in natural language or vice versa, creating splits that no monolingual tokenizer would produce. A beginner assumes tokenization is a neutral preprocessing step; an expert worries that the vocabulary allocation is a zero-sum competition between domains, so code-heavy corpora quietly starve natural language of efficient token representations for certain morphological patterns (and vice versa for numeric literals or operator sequences). The deeper concern is that these artifacts aren't uniformly distributed — they cluster around domain-boundary concepts like variable names that are also English words ("model", "loss", "head"), numeric expressions embedded in prose, and mixed-script identifiers, creating pockets of anomalously high fertility that the model must silently compensate for during training. Experts also worry about invisible corpus leakage: merge rules learned from one domain encode implicit structural assumptions that surface as subtle biases in how the model attends to and generates the other domain.

The dominant predictor is raw byte-pair frequency in the training corpus weighted by document count, not token utility — so if Python files constitute 30% of tokens but appear in tightly repetitive patterns (think self., def , return ), those merges can outcompete semantically richer English bigrams that appear less densely. GPT-2's tokenizer, trained on WebText, famously allocates tokens like Ġreturn and Ġself efficiently, but when CodeGen (Nijkamp et al., 2022) and early StarCoder models extended vocabularies to code, audits showed that common English morphological suffixes like -tion, -ment got fragmented in code-adjacent contexts because the merge budget was consumed by operator-identifier sequences. The measurable consequence of the "wrong" domain winning is elevated fertility: a word like "implementation" might tokenize as impl, em, ent, ation in a code-heavy vocabulary (four tokens) versus two tokens in a prose-native one, directly increasing sequence length and therefore attention cost quadratically for long documents. Fertility asymmetry also degrades next-token prediction calibration — the model must spread probability mass across more steps to reconstruct a single semantic unit, which Rust et al. (2021) in "How Good is Your Tokenizer?" showed correlates with downstream task accuracy drops of 3–8% on morphologically complex languages, a signal that almost certainly applies cross-domain as well. A subtler consequence is that the model's positional encoding sees the fragmented word at different relative positions depending on which domain context precedes it, so the same surface form gets inconsistent positional representations across the training distribution. The hardest-to-detect damage is in embedding space: tokens that "won" their merges from code carry code-corpus co-occurrence statistics into their initial embeddings, biasing their geometry before any fine-tuning occurs.

Practitioners do attempt this — the canonical example is LLaMA's vocabulary being extended for code or non-Latin scripts, and Meta's CodeLlama explicitly added tokens for common Python idioms — but the intervention creates an immediate embedding initialization problem: new tokens have no trained embedding vector, so they're typically initialized randomly or from a mean of related tokens, which means the model's residual stream has never seen that token's representation in any layer's weight matrix, and early fine-tuning steps are dominated by noisy gradient updates for those tokens rather than meaningful task learning. The second-order problem is tokenization inconsistency across the existing corpus: any text that was previously tokenized one way during pretraining is now tokenizable a different way, so if you retokenize fine-tuning data with the expanded vocabulary, you create a distribution mismatch between what the attention layers learned during pretraining and what they now receive — Hewitt et al. and others have noted this as a form of "vocabulary shift" that can silently degrade base capabilities. A related problem is fertility inversion: adding a long compound token (say, self.attention) reduces fertility for that sequence but increases it elsewhere because the merge ordering downstream is now disrupted — sequences that previously shared prefix tokens with the new entry now get split differently, fragmenting previously efficient representations. There's also a softmax pressure problem: the output projection matrix grows with vocabulary size, so each new token dilutes probability mass across the distribution, requiring the model to sharpen its logits to maintain the same top-1 accuracy — in practice this manifests as increased perplexity on the original domain immediately after vocabulary expansion, which Zoph et al. (2016) on transfer learning and more recently the Tokenizer Surgery paper (2024) both document. Finally, if the vocabulary expansion is done without retraining the full model — just fine-tuning — the new tokens never develop coherent long-range attention patterns, because the keys and queries in earlier layers were never trained to route information through those token identities, leaving them as embedding-space orphans that the model uses inconsistently.

When the model processes an orphan token in the forward pass, the residual stream at that position receives an embedding vector that lies off the manifold of the trained distribution — mechanistic interpretability work (Nostalgebraist's logit lens, and more formally Belrose et al. 2023's tuned lens) shows that such positions produce high-entropy, unstable intermediate logit distributions across layers, meaning early layers "don't know what to do" with the token and late layers overcorrect with sharp but poorly-calibrated predictions. Attention routing fails in a specific way: the query vector for an orphan token is a linear projection of an untrained embedding, so it produces dot products with key vectors that are effectively random relative to the trained key space — empirically this looks like diffuse, near-uniform attention patterns at that position, which you can observe directly from attention weight matrices without any interpretability tooling. The consequence in generation is that the model either avoids the token entirely (assigning it near-zero logit during sampling, which is why vocabulary-expanded models often fail to actually use new tokens without forced fine-tuning) or produces it in contextually incoherent positions because the output embedding matrix row for that token was initialized independently of the input embedding. From outside the weights, the most principled detection method is probing fertility-adjusted perplexity: tokenize a held-out corpus both with the original and expanded vocabulary, measure per-token cross-entropy specifically on positions where the two tokenizations diverge, and look for anomalously high loss variance at those positions — a signature that the model's predictions are unstable precisely where orphan tokens appear. A second external probe is embedding neighborhood analysis: project the new token's embedding into the pretrained embedding space using PCA or UMAP and measure its distance to its k-nearest neighbors; orphan tokens cluster in low-density regions with neighbors that are semantically incoherent, whereas well-integrated tokens have tight, semantically consistent neighborhoods that reflect their syntactic and semantic role. Google's PaLM 2 technical report alludes to exactly this problem when discussing vocabulary transfer across languages, noting that tokens added for new scripts required disproportionate compute to reach the same loss levels as native vocabulary tokens — a ratio they imply was around 3-5x more fine-tuning steps for equivalent calibration.

Yes, and the attack surface is more concrete than it might appear: an adversary who knows a model has undergone vocabulary expansion can craft inputs that force orphan tokens into high-stakes positions — specifically into the context window just before a safety-relevant decision or a factual claim — exploiting the fact that diffuse attention at that position degrades the model's ability to integrate preceding context, effectively creating a local amnesia that disrupts coherent reasoning precisely where it matters. This is structurally similar to the "token smuggling" class of attacks documented by Sztaki and others in 2023, where unusual tokenization boundaries cause safety classifiers to miss prohibited content because the classifier's token-level features don't align with the semantic boundary — orphan tokens amplify this because they additionally corrupt the residual stream state of neighboring positions through attention diffusion. A more systematic vulnerability exists in retrieval-augmented systems: if an attacker can influence the retrieved documents (e.g., via corpus poisoning), inserting sequences that tokenize to orphan tokens in the expanded vocabulary creates positions of high uncertainty that the model's generation head handles inconsistently, potentially biasing outputs in ways that are difficult to attribute to any single input span. The detectability of the signal cuts both ways — Anthropic's red-teaming work and Wallace et al.'s (2019) universal adversarial triggers research both suggest that gradient-based attack methods converge faster on token positions where the model's internal state is already high-entropy, meaning orphan tokens are essentially pre-softened attack targets that require fewer optimization steps to exploit. Concretely, a vocabulary-expanded model might be more vulnerable to prefix-injection attacks by a factor proportional to the number of orphan tokens in the injected prefix, because each one contributes independent attention noise that compounds across layers. The defense landscape is weak here: neither input filtering nor output monitoring easily catches this class of attack because the orphan tokens may be individually innocuous and the degradation they cause is statistical rather than symbolic, making it invisible to rule-based guardrails.

The implication holds broadly: any tokenization perturbation that moves the input sequence's token-position distribution away from the training manifold creates analogous instability, and this includes Unicode normalization mismatches, BPE dropout applied asymmetrically at inference, prompt templating that introduces separator tokens the base model never saw, and even mundane things like inconsistent whitespace handling between training and serving pipelines. The minimal condition for security relevance has three components: the perturbation must (1) produce a token sequence whose per-position embedding lies in a low-density region of the training distribution, (2) occur at a position that is causally upstream of a high-stakes output decision, and (3) produce different token boundaries than the "canonical" rendering of the same semantic content — that third condition is what enables the adversary to craft inputs that humans read one way and the model processes another. Karpathy's tokenization stress tests and Jiang et al.'s (2023) "Mistral" ablations both inadvertently demonstrate condition three: the same mathematical expression tokenizes differently depending on surrounding whitespace, and the model's numerical reasoning accuracy varies by up to 15% across these surface-identical inputs, which meets all three conditions for security relevance even without any adversarial intent. The homoglyph attack literature (Boucher et al. 2022, "Bad Characters") is the cleanest empirical proof of this framework: substituting visually identical Unicode characters forces different token boundaries, and they demonstrated code injection into model-generated outputs with success rates above 70% on several production systems — the attack works precisely because it satisfies all three conditions without triggering any semantic-level filter. A tokenization perturbation that only satisfies conditions one and two but not three is a reliability problem, not a security problem — it degrades performance but doesn't create an exploitable gap between human and model interpretation. The most underappreciated instantiation of this vulnerability is prompt template injection across API layers: when a user-facing API wraps user input in a system prompt template, the concatenation point often produces novel token boundaries that neither the base model's pretraining nor the template designer's testing ever covered, silently satisfying all three conditions at scale for every API call.

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-2323)

The most promising formal candidate is a semantic-tokenization divergence (STD) score defined as the KL divergence between the token boundary distribution produced by the model's tokenizer and a reference boundary distribution derived from a linguistically-motivated segmenter (spaCy morphemes, tree-sitter AST node boundaries for code, or a fast character-level language model) — when these two boundary distributions diverge significantly at a given input position, you have a quantifiable signal that the model is processing a different segmentation than a human or reference parser would expect. The computational bottleneck is the reference segmenter: spaCy runs at roughly 50k tokens/second on CPU, tree-sitter is faster but code-specific, and a character-level LM adds a full forward pass — none of these is free at inference time for high-throughput APIs, but the key insight is that you only need to compute STD on suspicious spans, not the full input, which reduces the problem to first identifying candidate spans via cheap heuristics (unusual Unicode ranges, high punctuation density, mixed-script sequences) and then running the divergence computation selectively. Google's Perspective API and Jigsaw's toxicity pipeline both use a structurally similar two-stage filter architecture — cheap lexical pre-screen followed by expensive semantic scoring — which demonstrates the pattern is production-viable at scale, and an STD-based security layer could slot into the same architecture. The harder problem is calibrating the threshold: STD scores will be elevated for legitimate code-switching, multilingual inputs, technical jargon, and proper nouns, so a naive threshold produces unacceptable false-positive rates — you'd need per-domain calibration curves, which Ribeiro et al.'s CheckList framework suggests requires roughly 500-1000 labeled examples per domain to reach stable precision-recall tradeoffs. A deployable approximation that sidesteps the calibration problem is tokenization consistency under perturbation: re-tokenize the input after applying five to ten canonical normalizations (Unicode NFC, whitespace collapsing, homoglyph substitution) and measure the edit distance between the resulting token sequences — inputs where this distance exceeds one to two tokens per hundred characters are flagged, no reference segmenter required, and the computation costs only a handful of tokenizer passes which run at megabytes-per-second. IBM's adversarial robustness toolbox and Microsoft's Counterfit both lack this specific metric as of their last public releases, representing a concrete gap where an STD-based module would add novel defensive coverage that existing tooling doesn't provide.

Yes, and the inversion is straightforward enough that it should be considered a near-term practical threat rather than a theoretical one: an attacker treats the tokenization consistency score as a black-box objective function, runs a cheap combinatorial search (simulated annealing or greedy beam search over Unicode substitutions, whitespace insertions, and homoglyph swaps) to maximize token-sequence edit distance under the constraint that human-readable semantics are preserved, and uses the resulting high-divergence string as an adversarial prefix — this requires no model weights, no gradients, and no API queries beyond what's needed to verify semantic preservation, making it a fully black-box attack. The efficiency is the alarming part: because the tokenizer is deterministic and public, the oracle is free to query, and Wallace et al.'s (2019) universal adversarial trigger work showed that even gradient-based attacks converge in hundreds to low thousands of steps — a gradient-free search over the discrete tokenization space with a cheap consistency oracle would likely converge faster for targeted high-divergence inputs because the search space is constrained to a small set of character-level operations. Concretely, the attack reduces to finding strings in the "tokenization fault zone" — the region of character space where small edits cause large token boundary shifts — and this zone is densely populated near mixed-script boundaries, numeric expressions, and operator-identifier junctions in code, meaning an attacker doesn't need to search randomly but can seed the search from known high-fertility character classes. Boucher et al.'s (2022) Bad Characters attack is essentially a manual version of this search, and they achieved code injection success rates above 70% with hand-crafted perturbations; an automated consistency-oracle-guided search would almost certainly achieve comparable or higher success rates with less human effort and broader target coverage. The minimal perturbation constraint — finding the smallest character-level change that maximally destabilizes — maps directly onto the L0 norm minimization framing from the adversarial examples literature, and Carlini and Wagner's (2017) C&W attack demonstrated that L0-constrained optimization in embedding space is tractable; the tokenization oracle replaces the embedding-space gradient with a discrete proxy that's cheaper to evaluate. The defense implication is that publishing tokenizer vocabularies and merge rules — which all major labs do for reproducibility — inadvertently hands attackers the complete specification of the fault zone map, and there's a real but underexplored tension between tokenizer transparency and adversarial robustness.
